generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, a presentation that delivers well has a structure the audience can follow: an introduction that frames the question, a main body that develops the argument in order, and a conclusion that leaves one clear message. Visual aids support that structure rather than replace it. A single clear image or figure lands faster than a paragraph of text, but a slide crammed with detail splits the audience between you and the screen. The slides prompt; you deliver.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students presenting on the same topic, with the same points to make.

Student A builds the slides first and lets them set the order. Each slide is full of text and detail, and the talk becomes a reading of the screen. The talk has no clear opening or close, so the audience is unsure what the main point means, and the slides pull their eyes away from Student A rather than supporting the argument. The material is all there, but it does not land.

Student B plans the structure first: an introduction that frames the question, a main body of three ordered points, and a conclusion with one clear message. Only then do the slides follow, each one a prompt or a single clear image. The audience can follow the argument, and the visual aids help it along. The delivery feels in control.

Both had the same points to make. Only Student B let a structure lead and made the visual aids serve it.
generatedProse.summary: A presentation delivers well when a clear structure leads it and the visual aids serve that structure. An introduction, an ordered main body and a conclusion give the audience a path through the material, and slides that prompt rather than script keep their attention on you. You can now build a supporting structure and design visual aids that back your argument. The final lesson looks at the errors that undo good preparation.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Student B's visual aids work better than Student A's?

items.text: They supported each point as prompts or a single clear image, rather than carrying dense text.
They used brighter colours and more animation.
More slides were used, so the audience saw more.
They were written out in full so they could be read aloud.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B's visual aids supported each point as prompts or a clear image, rather than carrying the talk.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the visual aids were doing, not how they looked.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B's visual aids worked because they prompted and supported each point. Colour, more slides or full text are not what made them effective.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
